newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-International Data sees stock offerings.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-International Data sees stock offerings.

text.p: International Data Group (IDG), a privately held publishing company, is launching a U.S. venture capital arm, setting up a mega-site on the World Wide Web and may soon start offering equity in its units to the public, its chairman said on Thursday.

Patrick McGovern, who founded IDG 33 years ago and built it into one of the world's leading publishers of computer-related periodicals, said the new Internet site would feature a rich electronic commerce component.
"We are focused on making our readers successful," he told Reuters in an interview at Herring Communication's Venture Market West in Monterey.

Boston-based IDG is also looking into raising capital by offering equity in certain of its operating units in the coming months, McGovern said. He said IDG group's International Data Corp research arm might be valued at four to 10 times revenues.
Such an offering would follow the successful public flotations of high technology consultancies Gartner Group and Forrester Research.

IDG is contemplating the sale of some 20 percent of IDC and a similar stake in the fast-growing IDG Books unit, whose more than 430 titles include the popular "...For Dummies" series, by next spring. At a valuation of $300 million, IDG Books could raise around $60 million, he said.

IDG this week is launching IDG Ventures, based in San Francisco, to invest a fund of $80 million in seed and early-phase start-up companies during the next five years, McGovern said. The fund will invest in Internet commerce systems and other tools aimed at Internet technology, which he said can facilitate "matching people with opportunities."

IDG established a venture capital fund in Japan 18 years ago. In 1994 it put up half the investment in a $120 million joint venture fund with the Chinese government to encourage business start-ups in that country's booming economy.

IDG publishes more than 275 periodicals reaching more than 70 million people in 82 countries and has launched 140 related Web sites. McGovern said IDG adds eight to 10 Web sites a month along with an average of two print titles a month.

The new Web mega-site, to be launched next month, will include separate services grouped by professional roles and help each group -- chief information officers, for example -- sift through IDG laboratory results, reviews and peer's comments to select products and services for purchase.
IDG also will provide updated data on current prices for products, along with appropriate terms and conditions and customer satisfaction data and qualify vendors to sell to its readers.

McGovern said IDG expects to be able to capture a percentage of transaction value, but is also looking at advertising rates graduated to provide higher revenues for those which prompt visitors to IDG's site to place orders.
By doing this, revenues per reader may be able to be increased by up to three to four times, he said.
Readers will benefit from discounts on membership fees, for example, and other promotions, such as a "frequent-flyer" type program.

In January, McGovern demonstrated his determination to spread publications to far reaches of the globe, tracing the expansion of the computer industry, when he traveled to the South Pole to launch Computerworld Antarctica. Now he said IDG truly reaches to the seven continents of the world.
IDG's revenues in 1996 were $1.7 billion, and the company employs more than 8,500, the company said. ((sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto Bureau, 415 846 5400))
